summary: Describes the External Data Representation (XDR) standard, a way to write data in a form independent of the machine, as it is deployed and accepted. It replaces RFC 1832. It is an Internet Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Computers store numbers differently. XDR is a shared way of writing them down so any two machines read the same thing.

subtitle: A language and a byte layout that let machines with different architectures exchange the same data.

tldr.problem: Different computer architectures store data differently, so raw memory cannot simply be copied from one machine to another.
tldr.mechanism: XDR gives a small C-like language to describe data, and a fixed encoding in which every item takes a multiple of four bytes, with a single byte order and implicit typing.
tldr.outcome: XDR describes the data formats of protocols such as ONC RPC and NFS. RFC 4506 makes no technical changes to RFC 1832, which it obsoletes.

today: RFC 4506 is an Internet Standard that obsoletes RFC 1832 and has not itself been obsoleted or updated. It adds no technical change to RFC 1832; it adds IANA and security text and separates normative from informative references.

sections.title: What XDR Is For
sections.content:
XDR (External Data Representation) is a standard for the description and encoding of data. It is useful for moving data between different computer architectures, and the RFC says it has been used between machines as different as the SUN WORKSTATION, VAX, IBM-PC and Cray.

XDR uses a language to describe data formats. The language describes data only: it is not a programming language. It is similar to C, and protocols such as ONC RPC (Remote Procedure Call) and NFS use it to describe the format of their data. XDR fits into the ISO presentation layer and uses implicit typing, unlike X.409, which uses explicit typing.

The one assumption XDR makes is that bytes (octets, 8 bits) are portable between devices.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine two friends who speak different languages. XDR is a shared picture dictionary they both agree to use, so a message means the same thing to both.

sections.title: The Four-Byte Block
sections.content:
Every XDR item takes up a multiple of four bytes (32 bits). Bytes are numbered 0 through n-1 and written to a byte stream so that byte m always comes before byte m+1. If the n bytes of data are not a multiple of four, they are followed by 0 to 3 zero bytes of fill to reach one.

This rule is what makes the rest of the format simple: every type is built from four-byte units, and a reader can always find where the next item starts.

RFC 4506 itself makes no technical changes to RFC 1832. It was published to note IANA considerations, augment the security considerations and separate normative from informative references.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything is packed into boxes that hold four bytes each. If a thing does not fill its last box, the empty space is filled with zeros.

sections.title: Numbers and Booleans
sections.content:
An XDR int is a 32-bit two's complement number in the range -2147483648 to 2147483647, with byte 0 the most significant. An unsigned int covers 0 to 4294967295. A hyper and an unsigned hyper are the same idea at 64 bits (8 bytes).

An enum has the same representation as a signed integer, and it is an error to encode any integer that the enum declaration did not assign. A bool is the enum with FALSE = 0 and TRUE = 1.

Floating-point numbers follow IEEE 754: float is 32 bits (1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits biased by 127, 23 fraction bits), double is 64 bits (11 exponent bits biased by 1023, 52 fraction bits) and quadruple is 128 bits (15 exponent bits biased by 16383, 112 fraction bits). A NaN is system dependent and must not be read as anything other than NaN.
sections.plainLanguage: A whole number always gets the same size box, whether it is small or big, and the biggest digit always comes first. Decimal numbers use a standard recipe that all computers know.

sections.title: Opaque Data, Strings and Arrays
sections.content:
Opaque data is uninterpreted bytes. Fixed-length opaque data is declared opaque identifier[n];. Variable-length data is declared opaque identifier<m>; and is encoded as the length n (an unsigned integer), then the n bytes, then fill to a multiple of four. If the maximum m is left out, it is assumed to be (2**32) - 1.

A string is encoded the same way as variable-length opaque data, as a count followed by ASCII bytes. Encoding a length greater than the declared maximum is an error.

Arrays of one element type are encoded element by element. A fixed-length array is declared type-name identifier[n];. A variable-length array carries an element count first and is declared type-name identifier<m>;. Elements share a type but may differ in size, as with an array of strings.
sections.plainLanguage: For a word or a list, XDR first says how long it is, then gives the contents, then pads out the last box with zeros.

sections.title: Structures, Unions and Optional Data
sections.content:
A struct is encoded by writing its components in the order they were declared. A discriminated union is a discriminant (an int, unsigned int or enumerated type such as bool) followed by the one arm that the discriminant value selects. A default arm is optional; without it, unspecified discriminant values are not valid. A void is a zero-byte quantity, handy for union arms that carry no data.

Optional data is written type-name *identifier;. It is a union on a bool: TRUE followed by the element, or FALSE followed by nothing. The RFC notes it is the same as a variable-length array with a maximum of 1, and it is the preferred way to describe recursive structures such as linked lists and trees.

A const gives a symbolic name to a number and declares no data. A typedef defines a new type name, and the RFC prefers the form enum bool { ... }; over typedef enum { ... } bool; because the type name is seen first.
sections.plainLanguage: A struct is a form with boxes filled in order. A union is a form where the first box says which kind of form follows. Optional data is a box that says yes or no before the thing itself.

sections.title: Why XDR Looks the Way It Does
sections.content:
Section 5 of the RFC answers design questions directly. A language beats diagrams because it is more formal, less ambiguous and closer to C or Pascal, which makes encoders and decoders easier to write.

  • One byte order, big-endian. Two orders would need a higher-level protocol to say which is in use, and XDR is not a protocol. The RFC admits this is unfair to little-endian machines, but one order means being unfair to somebody.
  • Four-byte unit. A smaller unit makes data smaller but causes alignment problems; a larger one aligns everywhere but bloats the data. Four is the compromise.
  • Zero padding. The same data should encode to the same bytes on every machine, so encoded data can be compared or checksummed.
  • No explicit typing. Type fields cost space and interpretation time, and most protocols already know what they expect.

The RFC also lists what XDR lacks: bit fields, bitmaps and packed decimals.
sections.plainLanguage: The designers picked one way of doing each thing so nobody has to ask how a message is written. Picking one is a little unfair to some computers, but it keeps everything simple.

sections.title: The XDR Language and an Example
sections.content:
The language is specified in an extended Backus-Naur Form. Comments start with /* and end with */, and identifiers are case sensitive. The keywords include bool, case, const, default, double, quadruple, enum, float, hyper, int, opaque, string, struct, switch, typedef, union, unsigned and void.

The worked example describes a file with a name, a kind (TEXT = 0, DATA = 1, EXEC = 2), an owner and its data. A file named sillyprog owned by john, holding the 6 bytes (quit) and run by lisp, is shown encoded as a series of four-byte words, each length followed by its characters and zero fill.
sections.plainLanguage: XDR comes with its own little language for writing down what a message looks like, like a recipe card. The example shows a recipe for a file and the exact bytes you would get from it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
XDR is a data description language, not a protocol, so it has no security considerations of its own. Protocols that carry XDR, such as NFSv4, must provide security services for the data they transport. Encoders and decoders must still be written with care. The RFC lists these known risks:

  • Buffer overflow. Protocols should use explicit limits (<value>) rather than <> where feasible, and decoders must check incoming sizes against their buffers.
  • Nul bytes inside strings. A decoder using nul-terminated strings may see a shorter apparent size, which can cause memory leaks and denial of service.
  • Characters illegal for the application, such as / in a file name component.
  • Recursive decoders. A long linked list of optional data can overflow the stack, so decoders and encoders should be non-recursive or limit list length.
sections.plainLanguage: XDR is just the writing rules, so any safety checks belong to whoever reads the message. A careful reader checks that nothing is too long or odd before using it.
